title: Data Center Energy Trends Force a Rethink of Chip Power Delivery
gist: Summarizing Intel Foundry's two-part series, the article argues AI data center growth makes chip power delivery central, citing Gartner forecasts of data center power rising from 104 GW in 2025 to 290 GW by 2030. Intel's answers are backside power on 18A with on-die capacitors, plus voltage conversion moved close to the load via integrated regulators and regulator chiplets.

insights.claim: Intel Foundry cites Gartner estimates that worldwide data center power demand will rise from 104 gigawatts in 2025 to 132 gigawatts in 2026, reaching 290 gigawatts by 2030.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Power availability is becoming a binding constraint on compute expansion.

insights.claim: AI-optimized servers are expected to account for 31% of data center power consumption in 2026 and surpass conventional servers by 2027.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: AI mix shift drives the growth in power need.

insights.claim: Computing expansion depends on available electricity and cooling capacity, so operators must split limited power budgets among processors, memory, networking and storage; better power delivery could raise useful output within those budgets.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Power delivery efficiency becomes an infrastructure economics issue, not only a chip design one.

insights.claim: Conventional frontside power delivery shares metal layers between power and signals; rising current increases resistive voltage loss and inductance complicates responses to workload changes, forcing wider connections, extra capacitors and operating margins.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Margins spent on power delivery cost efficiency and performance.

insights.claim: Intel's RibbonFET gate-all-around architecture with Intel 18A moves power routing to the chip backside, creating shorter paths to transistors and freeing frontside resources for signals, which Intel says reduces resistance, inductance and IR drop.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Backside power is a differentiator Intel promotes for foundry customers.

insights.claim: Intel Foundry describes Omni MIM on-die capacitors, substrate-embedded capacitors with through-silicon vias and embedded deep trench capacitors that supply nearby charge on sudden demand, limiting brief voltage dips for bursty AI inference and HPC workloads.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Local charge storage lets designers use less conservative operating settings.

insights.claim: Combining multiple dies concentrates current demand and increases the number of voltage domains, and package connections must carry power alongside dense signal traffic, so advanced packaging can create electrical bottlenecks.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Packaging gains in bandwidth bring power delivery penalties that must be solved.

insights.claim: Distributing power at a higher voltage reduces the current needed for a given power, with conversion near the compute die supplying the lower operating voltage; the benefit depends on regulator efficiency and the full delivery network.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Moving conversion close to the load is the core architectural shift.

insights.claim: Intel describes fully integrated voltage regulators supported by CoaxMIL magnetic inductors, continuous capacitive voltage regulators (C2VR) that use capacitors instead of inductors, and dedicated regulator chiplets placed beneath compute dies or within package structures.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Gives a menu of regulator implementations with different placement flexibility.

insights.claim: A processor cannot consistently exploit its capabilities if supply voltage fluctuates beyond acceptable limits, and better routing, localized charge storage and nearby regulation could reduce the margins required for safe operation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Power integrity translates directly into usable performance and efficiency.

insights.claim: Scaling computation now requires coordinated advances across transistors, wiring, capacitors, regulators and packaging, and power delivery is becoming a decisive factor in whether additional silicon yields worthwhile performance under constrained energy budgets.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Competitive advantage shifts to system-level power co-design.
